newsitem.title: UK: New UK foreign secretary is fiery debater.
newsitem.headline: New UK foreign secretary is fiery debater.

text.p: New British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook is a feared political operator widely regarded as a superb debater and one of the most intelligent men in parliament.

A diminutive figure with a bright red beard, he told reporters within minutes of his appointment that he intended to repair relations with the European Union which frayed badly during the last years of Conservative rule.
But question marks remained over his dedication to his new post since it was an open secret that he would rather be Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister).

Cook belongs to the traditional left wing of the Labour party but has good relations with its modernising leader, Tony Blair, who discarded much of the movement's socialist tenets since taking charge in 1994.
The 51-year-old Scotsman, who enjoys wide respect among the party's left wing, is a prickly man with a small circle of close friends and refers good-humouredly to his lack of "classic good looks".
One of his finest moments came in February last year when parliament debated a report on arms sales to Iraq before the 1991 Gulf War.

Cook was given a copy of the report only an hour before the debate but absorbed enough data to launch an damning assault on the government which Blair described as one of the most brilliant performances in his parliamentary career.
For the time being Cook has focused on the task ahead by talking about how he plans to smooth Britain's relations with the European Union, which sank to rock bottom under the Conservatives.
He still stays true to the internationalist roots of old Labour, which eschewed militarism and the arms trade, and says he wants to improve the role of the Commonwealth.
Though there is little chance of Cook becoming chancellor in the foreseeable future, hardly a day goes by without fresh speculation about what he might end up doing.

Cook is a keen fan of parliamentary reform and together with the minority Liberal Democrats worked out plans to revolutionise politics by holding a referendum on adopting proportional representation and backing devolution for Scotland and Wales.
Some in the party say they would not be surprised to see him as the head of a Scottish parliament or even de facto leader of a sovereign Scotland -- rumours Cook has done nothing to dispel.
Robert Finlayson Cook was born on February 28, 1946, and is married with two children. He is a fanatic horse racing fan and writes a regular tipster's guide for the Glasgow Herald newspaper.
